title: How To Repair A Broken Relationship With Your Students ur-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a recovery plan for teachers who lose their cool, raise their voice, or otherwise damage trust with their class. He advises waiting until the next morning to address it, then briefly and directly admitting the mistake — 'I lost my cool and I'm sorry' — and letting the apology sink in without over-explaining. He also insists on still holding students accountable for the behavior that triggered the outburst, avoiding the temptation to win them back with fun activities or eased standards, which he calls manipulative. Trust, he explains, is rebuilt slowly through consistent, calm, day-by-day behavior rather than grand gestures. The article closes by tying this recovery advice back to the core lesson of never letting minor misbehavior slide to the point that it triggers an emotional outburst in the first place.
points: Wait until the next morning to address an outburst, giving both teacher and students a fresh start.
A brief, direct apology — admitting the mistake without over-explaining — models accountability for students.
Still hold students accountable for the behavior that triggered the outburst; apologizing doesn't erase their responsibility.
Avoid trying to win students back with fun activities or eased standards, which is manipulative and cheapens the relationship.
Trust rebuilds slowly through consistent, calm, day-by-day behavior, not through grand gestures.
quotes: It’s best to wait until the next morning before addressing the incident that precipitated your outburst.
Say simply, “Yesterday I was unhappy with the way you behaved during math, and I handled it poorly. I lost my cool and I’m sorry.
Now is your opportunity to do what you should have done instead of losing your cool. Hold your students accountable for the previous days’ behavior.
Resist the urge to try to win them back with a fun afternoon, a silly game, or an easing of your behavior standards. These methods are manipulative.
Trust is built over time with your consistent behavior. It’s an hour-by-hour, day-by-day sameness that restores rapport and influence.
One of the keys to keeping your cool is to never let behavior reach the point where it gets under your skin.
